separable: no object — *the kids are acting up*; nothing ever stands between *act* and *up*
gloss: To behave badly, especially of a child who wants attention.
examples: The twins *act up* every time we have company.
He *acted up* in class all week and lost recess.
She's been *acting up* ever since the baby came home.

ru: барахлить, забарахлить; давать сбои; ныть (о больном месте)
separable: no object — *the printer is acting up*; the two words never come apart
gloss: To start working badly or hurting, of a machine or a part of the body.
examples: My knee *acts up* when it rains.
The printer *acted up* again this morning.
The old furnace has been *acting up* all winter.
contrast: One verb, two lives: a child *acts up* and a car *acts up*. Only the subject tells you whether it is bad behavior or a breakdown.

separable: separable — *act out the scene*, and *act it out*; a pronoun has to go in the middle
gloss: To perform something as a scene, showing it with actions instead of telling it.
examples: The kids *act out* the whole story with puppets.
She *acted out* the argument for us, doing both voices.
They were *acting out* the scene when the lights went out.

ru: срываться, сорваться; выплёскивать эмоции в плохом поведении
separable: no object — *he's acting out*; in this meaning the verb stands alone
gloss: To behave badly because of feelings you cannot put into words.
examples: Kids often *act out* when their parents separate.
He *acted out* for months after the move.
The counselor says she's *acting out*, not turning mean.
contrast: With an object it means 'perform': *act out a scene*. With no object it means 'misbehave out of hurt' — the object is the whole difference.

ru: действовать по (совету, информации); принимать меры, принять меры
separable: inseparable — *act on the advice*, never *act the advice on*
gloss: To do something because of advice, information, or an order you have been given.
examples: We *act on* every complaint we get.
The police *acted on* an anonymous tip.
He's finally *acting on* his doctor's advice.

separable: separable — *add up the numbers*, and *add them up*
gloss: To find the total of a set of numbers.
examples: *Add up* the column and tell me what you get.
She *added up* the receipts twice.
I'm still *adding up* what the trip cost us.

separable: no object — *his story doesn't add up*
gloss: To make sense, said most often when something does not.
examples: His story just doesn't *add up*.
Nothing she told the police *added up*.
The numbers weren't *adding up*, so they ordered an audit.
contrast: Usually negative: *it doesn't add up*. In the affirmative Americans say *that adds up* to mean 'that figures, that explains it'.

separable: no object — *the little charges add up*
gloss: To grow into a large amount through many small ones.
examples: Three dollars a day doesn't sound like much, but it *adds up*.
The late fees *added up* fast.
Those extra hours have been *adding up* all month.

ru: составлять, составить (в сумме); сводиться, свестись к
separable: inseparable — all three words stay together and the total follows *to*: *it adds up to nothing*, never *add it up to*
gloss: To come to a total, or to amount to a particular result.
examples: The bills *add up to* almost two thousand dollars.
All that work *added up to* nothing.
Everything he's told us is *adding up to* one thing: he's quitting.
contrast: *add up* on its own means 'make sense'; *add up to* names the sum or the upshot. The formal near-twin is *amount to*.

separable: separable — *add on a service charge*, and *add it on*
gloss: To charge or include something extra, on top of what is already there.
examples: They *add on* a twenty percent service charge for big parties.
The dealer *added on* four hundred dollars in fees.
We're *adding on* a delivery charge starting in June.
contrast: In American houses *add on* also means to build an extension: *they added on a bedroom over the garage*. The noun is *an add-on*, with a hyphen.

separable: separable — *add in the eggs*, and *add them in*
gloss: To include something in a mixture, a list, or a total you are putting together.
examples: *Add in* the chocolate chips at the very end.
They *added in* two more names at the last minute.
Don't forget you're *adding in* tax and tip.

separable: separable — *air out the bedroom*, and *air it out*
transitivity: both — transitive (air out the closet), intransitive (let the tent air out)
gloss: To let fresh air into a room or through cloth to get rid of a smell or dampness.
examples: Open the windows and *air out* the bedroom.
She *aired out* the sleeping bags on the porch.
The basement has been *airing out* since Tuesday.

separable: separable — *amp up the pressure*, and *amp it up*
gloss: To increase something in force, volume, or excitement.
examples: They *amp up* security every year for the parade.
The coach *amped up* the pressure in the fourth quarter.
The ads are *amping up* the hype for the sequel.
contrast: Also heard as an adjective: *the crowd was amped up* — keyed up, excited. Informal but everywhere in American speech.

separable: inseparable — *angle for a raise*, never *angle a raise for*
gloss: To try to get something by hinting at it instead of asking straight out.
examples: He *angles for* a raise every time we talk.
They *angled for* a discount and got one.
She was *angling for* an invitation all evening.
contrast: From fishing — *angling* is fishing with a hook. The verb keeps the sense of baiting rather than asking.

separable: separable when there is an object — *answer me back*, never *answer back me*; most often there is no object at all: *don't answer back*
transitivity: both — transitive (don't answer me back), intransitive (don't answer back)
gloss: To reply rudely to someone who has authority over you.
examples: Don't *answer back* when your grandmother is talking.
He *answered back* and got sent to his room.
She's been *answering back* a lot lately.
contrast: *talk back* means exactly the same thing and is commoner in American speech: *don't talk back to me*.

separable: inseparable — *answer to the board*, never *answer the board to*
gloss: To be responsible to a person or group who can judge what you do.
examples: I *answer to* the regional manager, not to you.
He *answered to* no one for years.
Everyone here is *answering to* the same board now.
contrast: *answer to* someone is having a boss; *answer for* something is taking the blame for it: *he'll answer to the chief for what he did*.

ru: раскошеливаться, раскошелиться; вносить, внести свою долю
separable: inseparable — *ante up fifty dollars*, never *ante fifty dollars up*; most often there is no object at all
transitivity: both — transitive (ante up fifty dollars), intransitive (everybody has to ante up)
gloss: To pay the money you owe or the share that is expected of you.
examples: If you want in on the trip, *ante up*.
Each of us *anted up* fifty dollars.
The city is *anteing up* half the cost of the new field.
contrast: Watch the spelling: past *anted* (also written *anteed*), *-ing* form *anteing*. From poker, where the *ante* is what you put in before the cards are dealt.

separable: separable — *ask out a coworker*, and *ask her out*; with a pronoun it must split
gloss: To invite someone to go on a date.
examples: I'm going to *ask* her *out* this weekend.
He *asked out* a girl from his chemistry class.
She's been wanting to *ask* him *out* since September.
contrast: *ask someone out* is romantic; *ask someone over* is only an invitation to your house.

separable: no object — *ask around*; what you want to know follows *about*: *ask around about a good dentist*
gloss: To ask several different people about something, hoping one of them knows.
examples: Let me *ask around* and see if anyone has a truck.
I *asked around* at work and nobody had heard of it.
She's been *asking around* about a good dentist.

ru: справляться, справиться (о здоровье, о делах кого-л.)
separable: inseparable — *ask after your mother*, never *ask your mother after*
gloss: To ask how someone is, usually by asking a third person about them.
examples: Your mother *asked after* you at church.
He always *asks after* my father.
She was *asking after* the kids.
contrast: *ask after* someone is asking how they are; *ask for* someone is asking to speak to them: *a man called and asked for you*.

ru: приглашать, пригласить в гости (к себе домой)
separable: separable — *ask over a few friends*, and *ask them over*; with a pronoun it must split
gloss: To invite someone to come to your home.
examples: Let's *ask* the neighbors *over* for burgers.
They *asked* us *over* on Sunday.
She's *asking over* a few people from work.

separable: inseparable — *attend to the details*, never *attend the details to*
gloss: To deal with something that needs doing, or to take care of someone.
examples: I have a few things to *attend to* before we leave.
A nurse *attended to* him all night.
She's *attending to* the paperwork right now.
contrast: *attend a meeting* is plain *attend* — присутствовать. *attend to a matter* is this verb — заниматься. Dropping *to* changes the meaning completely.

ru: продавать, продать с аукциона; распродавать, распродать с молотка
separable: separable — *auction off the painting*, and *auction it off*
gloss: To sell something at an auction, usually to clear it out or raise money.
examples: The school *auctions off* the donated quilts every spring.
They *auctioned off* his tools after he died.
The bank is *auctioning off* the building next month.

ru: составлять, составить в среднем; выравниваться, выровняться
separable: separable when it takes an object — *average out the scores*, and *average them out*; with no object it stays whole and the figure follows *to* or *at*
transitivity: both — transitive (average out the scores), intransitive (it averages out to thirty dollars a week)
gloss: To come to a particular figure as an average, or to even out over time.
examples: It *averages out* to about thirty dollars a week.
The good months and the bad ones *averaged out* by December.
Once you've *averaged out* the bonuses, the pay is decent.
